title: حِكَايَةُ الْعَاشِقِ وَالْمَعْشُوقِ
titleEn: The Lover and the Beloved, continued
part: Night 110 · The Lover and the Beloved, continued
source: William Hay Macnaghten, ed., The Alif Laila, or Book of the Thousand Nights and One Night, vol. 1, Calcutta 1839 (“Calcutta II”), printed pp. 560–563 (Night 110, continuing directly from nights-109), transcribed from the 300 ppi scan (archive.org aliflailaorbooko01macn) by the editors' own transcription. The edition prints the prose essentially unpointed: ALL VOCALIZATION (tashkīl) IS EDITORIAL — ours, not the edition's — and the alphabet button strips it back to the bare rasm as Macnaghten prints it, except where a clear misprint has been corrected (each is noted). Romanization is simplified IJMES. Spelling, including the edition’s Middle Arabic forms, is preserved; clear misprints are corrected in the text, and the note on each gives the print’s reading. Obscure or doubtful forms are kept as printed, vocalized by evident sense and flagged in the notes. Read-aloud audio is a Modern Standard Arabic reading of this vocalised text, synthesized by machine, with word-by-word timing generated the same way.
about: Night 110 continues the story that the vizier Dandān tells within the tale of King ʿUmar ibn al-Nuʿmān, the story of the lover, the beloved and the go-between. Tāj al-Mulūk Khārān, now a master horseman, is so beautiful that poems are made about him; the night quotes five short poems on his beauty — four of them, after his first down appears at eighteen, on his cheek, his mole and his down — full of puns on Joseph, the caliph’s black banner, fire-worship, al-Khiḍr and the water of life. Companions gather round him hoping for office when he is sultan. He takes to hunting against his father’s wishes, rides out with his followers, and makes a great drive of game with nets, hounds, cheetahs and falcons, sending the best of the bag to his father. Next morning a merchant caravan halts by the same water; the prince has its goods laid out before him in a red satin tent, buys what pleases him, and as he turns to leave catches sight of a handsome young man among the merchants, pale with the grief of separation. As with every printed edition of the Nights, this one belongs to the late Egyptian recension (ZER) — an eighteenth-century expansion padded out to a literal 1001 nights; no printed edition is a medieval text, and Macnaghten regularised the language here and there, so some Middle Arabic texture is a nineteenth-century retrofit.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا كَانَتِ اللَّيْلَةُ الْعَاشِرَةُ بَعْدَ الْمِائَةِ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā kānati al-laylatu al-ʿāshiratu baʿda al-miʾati
sentences.l: And when it was the night, the tenth after the hundred,
sentences.i: And when it was the hundred and tenth night,

sentences.t: قَالَتْ بَلَغَنِي أَيُّهَا الْمَلِكُ السَّعِيدُ أَنَّ تَاجَ الْمُلُوكِ خَارَانَ ابْنَ الْمَلِكِ سُلَيْمَانَ شَاهْ لَمَّا مَهَرَ فِى الْفُرُوسِيَّةِ وَفَاقَ أَهْلَ زَمَانِهِ صَارَ مِنْ فَرْطِ جَمَالِهِ إِذَا خَرَجَ إِلَى بَعْضِ أَشْغَالِهِ يَفْتَتِنُ بِهِ كُلُّ مَنْ رَآهُ حَتَّى نَظَمُوا فِيهِ الْأَشْعَارَ وَتَهَتَّكَتْ فِي مَحَبَّتِهِ الْأَحْرَارُ لِمَا حَوَى مِنَ الْجَمَالِ الْبَاهِرِ كَمَا قَالَ فِيهِ الشَّاعِرُ
sentences.tr: qālat balaghanī ayyuhā al-maliku al-saʿīdu anna tāja al-mulūki khārāna ibna al-maliki sulaymāna shāh lammā mahara fī al-furūsiyyati wa-fāqa ahla zamānihi ṣāra min farṭi jamālihi idhā kharaja ilā baʿḍi ashghālihi yaftatinu bihi kullu man raʾāhu ḥattā naẓamū fīhi al-ashʿāra wa-tahattakat fī maḥabbatihi al-aḥrāru limā ḥawā mina al-jamāli al-bāhiri kamā qāla fīhi al-shāʿiru
sentences.l: She said: It has reached me, O king the happy, that Tāj al-Mulūk Khārān, son of the king Sulaymān Shāh, when he became-skilled in the horsemanship and surpassed the people of his time, became — from the excess of his beauty — (such that) when he went-out to some of his affairs, there was-enchanted by him everyone who saw him; until they composed about him the poems, and the free-born threw-off-restraint in love of him, for what he held of the dazzling beauty; as the poet said about him:
sentences.i: She said: It has reached me, O fortunate king, that when Tāj al-Mulūk Khārān, son of King Sulaymān Shāh, had mastered horsemanship and outshone everyone of his day, his beauty was so great that whenever he went out on any business of his, everyone who saw him was captivated. Poems were made about him, and free-born men threw off all restraint for love of him, so dazzling was the beauty he possessed. As the poet said of him:
sentences.n: Shahrazād takes up the night by repeating the end of the one before. ṣāra … idhā kharaja … yaftatinu, “he became (such that) whenever he went out … everyone was enchanted”: the sentence runs on loosely. tahattaka is “to cast off restraint, to be exposed to shame”, of lovers past caring who knows. li-mā, li- “because of” + mā “what”. al-ashʿār and al-aḥrār rhyme.

sentences.t:
عَانَقْتُهُ فَسَكِرْتُ مِنْ طِيبِ الشَّذَى * غُصْنًا رَطِيبًا بِالنَّسِيمِ قَدِ اغْتَذَى
سَكْرَانُ مَاشَرِبَ الْمُدَامَ وَانَّمَا * اَمْسَى بِخَمْرِ رُضَابِهِ مُتَنَبِّذَا
اَضْحَى الْجَمَالُ بِاَسْرِهِ فِي اَسْرِهِ * فَلِاَجْلِ ذَاكَ عَلَى الْقُلُوبِ اسْتَحْوَذَا
وَاللّٰهِ مَا خَطَرَ السُّلُوُّ بِخَاطِرِي * مَادُمْتُ فِي قَيْدِ الْحَيوةِ وَلَا اِذَا
انْ عِشْتُ عِشْتُ عَلَى هَوَاهُ وَاِنْ اَمُتْ * وَجْدًا بِهِ وَصَبَابَةً يَا حَبَّذَا
sentences.tr:
ʿānaqtuhu fa-sakirtu min ṭībi al-shadhā * ghuṣnan raṭīban bi-al-nasīmi qadi ightadhā
sakrānu mā shariba al-mudāma wa-innamā * amsā bi-khamri ruḍābihi mutanabbidhā
aḍḥā al-jamālu bi-asrihi fī asrihi * fa-li-ajli dhāka ʿalā al-qulūbi istaḥwadhā
wa-allāhi mā khaṭara al-sulūwu bi-khāṭirī * mā dumtu fī qaydi al-ḥayāti wa-lā idhā
in ʿishtu ʿishtu ʿalā hawāhu wa-in amut * wajdan bihi wa-ṣabābatan yā ḥabbadhā
sentences.l:
I embraced him, and I became-drunk from the sweetness of the fragrance — a bough, supple, that by the breeze has been-nourished.
Drunk — he drank not the wine; but rather he came-to-evening, by the wine of his saliva, steeped-like-date-wine.
The beauty, in its entirety, has come-to-be in his captivity; and for the sake of that, over the hearts he has gained-mastery.
By God, the consolation has not crossed my mind as long as I remain in the fetter of the life, nor then.
If I live, I live upon his love; and if I die of passion for him and longing — O how fine!
sentences.i:
I held him close and grew drunk on the sweetness of his scent — a tender bough the breeze had nourished.
Drunk, though he never drank wine: by evening the wine of his own lips’ dew had steeped him.
All of beauty, entire, is his captive, and so he has made himself master of every heart.
By God, forgetting him has never crossed my mind while I stay bound by life — nor will it then.
If I live, I live on love of him; and if I die of passion and longing for him — how sweet that would be!
sentences.n: The print has اسُّلُوُّ, a misprint for السُّلُوُّ, al-sulūw, “consolation, getting over a love”, corrected here. bi-asrihi … fī asrihi plays on asr, “entirety” (bi-asrihi, “all of it”), and asr, “captivity”. mutanabbidhā is rare: from nabīdh, date-wine, “turned to wine, steeped like nabīdh”; whose drunkenness the second line means, the youth’s or the poet’s, it leaves open. wa-lā idhā, “nor then”, is elliptic, probably “nor when I am no longer living”. The print leaves the alif of wa-innamā (وَانَّمَا) bare, without hamza or kasra, and likewise the alif of in, “if”, at the head of the last line. The rhyme is -dhā throughout.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا بَلَغَ مِنَ الْعُمْرِ ثَمَانِيَةَ عَشَرَعَامًا دَبَّ عِذَارُهُ الْأَخْضَرُ عَلَى شَامَةِ خَدِّهِ الْأَحْمَرِ وَزَانَهُمَا خَالٌ كَنُقْطَةِ عَنْبَرٍ وَصَارَ يَسْبِي الْعُقُولَ وَالنَّوَاظِرَ كَمَا قَالَ فِيهِ الشَّاعِرُ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā balagha mina al-ʿumri thamāniyata ʿashara ʿāman dabba ʿidhāruhu al-akhḍaru ʿalā shāmati khaddihi al-aḥmari wa-zānahumā khālun ka-nuqṭati ʿanbarin wa-ṣāra yasbī al-ʿuqūla wa-al-nawāẓira kamā qāla fīhi al-shāʿiru
sentences.l: And when he reached, of the age, eighteen years, his cheek-down, the green, crept over the mark of his cheek, the red; and there adorned the two of them a mole like a drop of ambergris; and he began to take-captive the minds and the eyes; as the poet said about him:
sentences.i: When he reached eighteen, the green down of his first beard crept over his rosy cheek, a beauty-spot like a drop of ambergris set both off, and he began to take minds and eyes captive. As the poet said of him:
sentences.n: The print runs عشر عاما, ʿashara ʿāman, together (عشرعاما). ʿidhār is the first down on a youth’s cheek, which the poets call “green”, meaning dark. shāma and khāl both mean a mole or beauty-spot; shāmat khaddihi seems to mean the fair surface of the cheek rather than a second mole. ka-, “like”: ka-nuqṭati ʿanbarin, “like a drop of ambergris”. Rhymed prose: al-akhḍar, al-aḥmar, ʿanbar.

sentences.t:
اَضْحَى لِيُوسُفَ فِى الْجَمَالِ خَلِيفَةً * تَخْشَاهُ كُلُّ الْعَاشِقِينَ اِذَا بَدَا
عَرِّجْ مَعِي وَانْظُرْ اِلَيْهِ لِكَيْ تَرَى * فِي خَدِّهِ عَلَمَ الْخِلَافَةِ اَسْوَداً
sentences.tr:
aḍḥā li-yūsufa fī al-jamāli khalīfatan * takhshāhu kullu al-ʿāshiqīna idhā badā
ʿarrij maʿī wa-unẓur ilayhi li-kay tarā * fī khaddihi ʿalama al-khilāfati aswadan
sentences.l:
He has become, to Joseph, in the beauty, a successor; all the lovers fear him when he appears.
Turn-aside with me and look at him, so that you see on his cheek the banner of the caliphate, black.
sentences.i:
In beauty he has become Joseph’s successor; every lover fears him when he appears.
Come aside with me and look at him, and you will see on his cheek the caliphate’s banner — black.
sentences.n: Joseph (Yūsuf) is the pattern of male beauty in the Qurʾān and the poets. khalīfa, “successor”, is also “caliph”, and the second line takes up the pun: black was the colour of the ʿAbbāsid caliphs’ banners, and the dark down on his cheek is that banner. li-, “to”: li-yūsufa khalīfatan, “a successor to Joseph”. aswad does not normally take tanwīn; the print’s tanwīn sits on the rhyme alif, read aswadā at the pause. The rhyme is -dā.

sentences.t: وَكَمَا قَالَ الْآخَرُ
sentences.tr: wa-kamā qāla al-ākharu
sentences.l: And as the other said:
sentences.i: And as another said:

sentences.t:
مَا اَبْصَرَتْ عَيْنَاكَ اَحْسَنُ مَنْظَرًا * فِيمَا يُرَى مِنْ سَائِرِ الْاَشْيَاءِ
كَالشَّامَةِ الْخَضْرَاءِ فَوْقَ الْوَجْنَةِ * الْحَمْرَاءِ تَحْتَ الْمُقْلَةِ السَّوْدَاءِ
sentences.tr:
mā abṣarat ʿaynāka aḥsanu manẓaran * fīmā yurā min sāʾiri al-ashyāʾi
ka-al-shāmati al-khaḍrāʾi fawqa al-wajnati * al-ḥamrāʾi taḥta al-muqlati al-sawdāʾi
sentences.l:
Your two eyes have not beheld (one) more beautiful of sight, among what is seen of all the things,
like the mole, the green, above the cheek, the red, beneath the eyeball, the black.
sentences.i:
Of all the things there are to see, your eyes have never seen a lovelier sight
than the green mole on the red cheek, below the black eye.
sentences.n: The print points aḥsanu with a ḍamma, where the grammar wants aḥsana, the object of “beheld”; the transliteration follows the print. ka-, “like”, stands where English needs “than”: nothing lovelier to compare with the green mole. The second line divides its hemistichs in the middle of the phrase al-wajnati al-ḥamrāʾi, “the red cheek”. Green, red and black are the down, the cheek and the eye.

sentences.t: وَكَمَا قَالَ الْآخَرُ
sentences.tr: wa-kamā qāla al-ākharu
sentences.l: And as the other said:
sentences.i: And as another said:

sentences.t:
عَجِبْتُ بِخَالٍ يَعْبُدُ النَّارَ دَائِمًا * بِخَدِّكَ لَمْ يُحْرَقْ بِهَا وَهْوَ كَافِرُ
وَاَعْجَبُ مِنْ ذَا اَنَّ بِاللَّحْظِ مُرْسَلًا * يُصَدِّقُ بِالْايَاتِ وَهْوَ لَسَاحِرُ
وَمَا اخْضَرَّ ذَاكَ الْخَدُّ نَبْتًا وَاِنَّمَا * لِكَثْرَةِ مَا شُقَّتْ عَلَيْهِ الْمَرَائِرُ
sentences.tr:
ʿajibtu bi-khālin yaʿbudu al-nāra dāʾiman * bi-khaddika lam yuḥraq bihā wa-hwa kāfiru
wa-aʿjabu min dhā anna bi-al-laḥẓi mursalan * yuṣaddiqu bi-al-āyāti wa-hwa la-sāḥiru
wa-mā ikhḍarra dhāka al-khaddu nabtan wa-innamā * li-kathrati mā shuqqat ʿalayhi al-marāʾiru
sentences.l:
I marvelled at a mole that worships the fire always on your cheek — it is not burned by it, and it is an unbeliever.
And more marvellous than this: that in the glance (there is) a sent-one who affirms the signs, and he is indeed a sorcerer.
And that cheek did not turn-green as growth; but rather for the many gall-bladders that have been split over it.
sentences.i:
I marvel at a mole that worships the fire on your cheek forever and is never burned by it, though it is an unbeliever.
Stranger still: in your glance there is a prophet who professes the signs — and he is a sorcerer.
That cheek did not turn green with growing down; no — it is from all the gall-bladders that have burst over it.
sentences.n: The mole is a fire-worshipper (a Zoroastrian) at the flame of the cheek, and an unbeliever ought to burn. In the second line mursal, “one sent”, is a prophet; the āyāt are the signs that prove a prophet, and sorcery is the charge his enemies bring against him — the glance is both. In the third, a lover dies of grief “with his gall-bladder burst”, and its green bile is what has coloured the cheek. ʿajibtu bi- stands for the usual ʿajibtu min, “marvel at”; bi-khaddika, bi- “on”: “on your cheek”; ṣaddaqa bi-, “believe in, affirm”. wa-hwa is a poetic shortening of wa-huwa. The rhyme is -ru.

sentences.t: وَكَمَا قَالَ الْآخَرُ
sentences.tr: wa-kamā qāla al-ākharu
sentences.l: And as the other said:
sentences.i: And as another said:

sentences.t:
اِنِّي لَاَعْجَبُ مِنْ سُؤَالِ النَّاسِ عَنْ * مَاءِ الْحَيوةِ بِاَيِّ اَرْضٍ مُنْهَمِرِ
وَلَقَدْ اَرَاهُ بِثَغْرِ ظَبْيٍ اَغْيَدٍ * حُلْوُ اللَّمَى وَعَلَيْهِ شَارِبُهُ الْخَضِرْ
وَمِنَ الْعَجَائِبِ اَنَّ مُوسَى يَلْتَقِي * مَعَهُ هُنَاكَ سَوُءِ لَمْ يَصْطَبِرْ
sentences.tr:
innī la-aʿjabu min suʾāli al-nāsi ʿan * māʾi al-ḥayāti bi-ayyi arḍin munhamiri
wa-laqad arāhu bi-thaghri ẓabyin aghyadin * ḥulwu al-lamā wa-ʿalayhi shāribuhu al-khaḍir
wa-mina al-ʿajāʾibi anna mūsā yaltaqī * maʿahu hunāka sawuʾi lam yaṣṭabir
sentences.l:
Indeed I marvel at the people’s asking about the water of the life — in which land (is it) pouring-forth —
when I do see it in the mouth of a gazelle, supple-necked, sweet of the dark-lip, and upon it his moustache, the green.
And among the wonders: that Moses meets with him there … did not have-patience.
sentences.i:
I wonder at people asking in what land the water of life wells up,
when I can see it in the mouth of a slender-necked gazelle, sweet of dark lip, with his green moustache standing over it.
And the wonder of it: Moses meets him there and … cannot be patient.
sentences.n: The poem plays on the legend of the water of life, guarded by al-Khiḍr, “the Green One”, and on Qurʾān 18, where Moses travels with al-Khiḍr and cannot bear patiently with him (lam yaṣṭabir). The youth’s mouth is the spring and his dark down is “the green one” standing over it. mūsā is also the common word for a razor: the razor meets the moustache and cannot hold back. The last hemistich is damaged in the print: سَوُءِ makes no sense that fits, so it is kept as printed and left untranslated (…). ḥulwu, “sweet”, is pointed nominative where the grammar wants ḥulwi, agreeing with ẓabyin; munhamiri is genitive, agreeing with arḍin. laqad arāhu, “I do see it”: laqad with the present verb, for emphasis. bi-, “in”: bi-ayyi arḍin, “in which land”; bi-thaghri, “in the mouth of”.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا صَارَ بِتِلْكَ الْحَالَةِ وَبَلَغَ مَبْلَغَ الرِّجَالِ زَادَ بِهِ الْجَمَالُ ثُمَّ صَارَ لِتَاجِ الْمُلُوكِ خَارَانَ أَصْحَابٌ وَأَحْبَابٌ وَكُلُّ مَنْ تَقَرَّبَ إِلَيْهِ يَرْجُوأَنَّهُ يَصِيرُ سُلْطَانًا بَعْدَ مَوْتِ أَبِيهِ وَأَنَّهُ يَكُونُ عِنْدَهُ أَمِيرًا
sentences.tr: fa-lammā ṣāra bi-tilka al-ḥālati wa-balagha mablagha al-rijāli zāda bihi al-jamālu thumma ṣāra li-tāji al-mulūki khārāna aṣḥābun wa-aḥbābun wa-kullu man taqarraba ilayhi yarjū annahu yaṣīru sulṭānan baʿda mawti abīhi wa-annahu yakūnu ʿindahu amīran
sentences.l: And when he came-to-be in that state, and reached the reaching-point of the men, the beauty increased in him; then there came-to-be for Tāj al-Mulūk Khārān companions and loved-ones, and everyone who drew-near to him was hoping that he would become sultan after the death of his father, and that he (himself) would be with him an emir.
sentences.i: When he had come to this and reached manhood, his beauty only grew; and Tāj al-Mulūk Khārān gathered companions and friends, every one of whom drew close to him hoping that he would be sultan after his father’s death and that he himself would be an emir at his side.
sentences.n: bi-, “in”: ṣāra bi-tilka al-ḥālati, “came to be in that state”; zāda bihi al-jamālu, “beauty increased in him”. li-, “for”: ṣāra li-X aṣḥābun, “there came to be companions for X”, he came to have them. The print runs يرجوانه, “hopes that he”, together. aṣḥāb and aḥbāb rhyme.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ إِنَّهُ تَعَلَّقَ بِالصَّيْدِ وَالْقَنَصِ وَصَارَ لَمْ يَفْتُرْ عَنْهُ سَاعَةً وَاحِدَةً وَكَانَ وَالِدُهُ الْمَلِكُ سُلَيْمَانُ شَاهْ يَنْهَاهُ عَنْ ذَلِكَ مَخَافَةً عَلَيْهِ مِنْ آفَاتِ الْبَرِّ وَالْوُحُوشِ فَلَمْ يَقْبَلْ مِنْهُ ذَلِكَ
sentences.tr: thumma innahu taʿallaqa bi-al-ṣaydi wa-al-qanaṣi wa-ṣāra lam yaftur ʿanhu sāʿatan wāḥidatan wa-kāna wāliduhu al-maliku sulaymānu shāh yanhāhu ʿan dhālika makhāfatan ʿalayhi min āfāti al-barri wa-al-wuḥūshi fa-lam yaqbal minhu dhālika
sentences.l: Then he became-attached to the hunting and the chase, and came-to-be — he did not slacken from it a single hour; and his father, the king Sulaymān Shāh, used to forbid him from that, out of fear for him of the perils of the open-country and the wild-beasts; but he did not accept that from him.
sentences.i: Then he took to hunting and the chase and never let up from it for a single hour. His father, King Sulaymān Shāh, kept forbidding it, fearing for him the dangers of the wilds and the wild beasts; but he would not listen to him in this.
sentences.n: The print has والدة, “mother”, a misprint for والده, “his father”, corrected here (the verb and the king’s name are masculine); and شاة, “sheep”, a misprint for شاه, Shāh, corrected here. taʿallaqa bi-, “become attached to”, the verb choosing the preposition. ṣāra lam yaftur, “he came to be not slackening”: ṣāra with a negated verb, a turn the text likes. ṣayd and qanaṣ are near-synonyms, “hunting and the chase”.

sentences.t: فَاتَّفَقَ أَنَّهُ قَالَ لِخُدَّامِهِ خُذُوا مَعَكُمْ عَلِيقَ عَشَرَةِ أَيَّامٍ فَامْتَثَلُوا مَا أَمَرَهُمْ بِهِ
sentences.tr: fa-ittafaqa annahu qāla li-khuddāmihi khudhū maʿakum ʿalīqa ʿasharati ayyāmin fa-imtathalū mā amarahum bihi
sentences.l: And it chanced that he said to his servants: Take with you fodder of ten days. And they complied-with what he commanded them (with).
sentences.i: It happened one day that he said to his servants, “Take ten days’ fodder with you,” and they did as he ordered.
sentences.n: ʿalīq is fodder for horses. li-, “to”: qāla li-khuddāmihi, “said to his servants”. amara bi-, “command (something)”: the verb chooses the preposition, so mā amarahum bihi is “what he commanded them”.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا خَرَجَ بِأَتْبَاعِهِ لِلصَّيْدِ وَالْقَنَصِ سَارُوا فِى الْبَرِّ وَلَمْ يَزَالُوا سَائِرِينَ أَرْبَعَةَ أَيَّامٍ حَتَّى أَشْرَفُوا عَلَى أَرْضٍ خَضْرَاءَ فَرَأَوْا فِيهَا وُحُوشًا رَاتِعَةً وَأَشْجَارًا يَانِعَةً وَعُيُونًا نَابِعَةً
sentences.tr: fa-lammā kharaja bi-atbāʿihi li-al-ṣaydi wa-al-qanaṣi sārū fī al-barri wa-lam yazālū sāʾirīna arbaʿata ayyāmin ḥattā ashrafū ʿalā arḍin khaḍrāʾa fa-raʾaw fīhā wuḥūshan rātiʿatan wa-ashjāran yāniʿatan wa-ʿuyūnan nābiʿatan
sentences.l: And when he went-out with his followers for the hunting and the chase, they journeyed in the open-country, and did not cease journeying four days, until they looked-down upon a land, green; and they saw in it wild-beasts grazing, and trees ripe, and springs welling.
sentences.i: When he rode out with his followers to hunt, they travelled through the wilds four days on end, until they came in sight of a green country, where they saw wild beasts grazing, trees heavy with fruit and springs welling up.
sentences.n: The print has فاما, a misprint for فلما, “and when”, and بانباعه, a misprint for باتباعه, “with his followers”, both corrected here. bi-, “with”: kharaja bi- is “go out with, take along”; li-, “for”: li-al-ṣaydi, “for the hunt”. ashrafa ʿalā, “to look down on, come in sight of”. rātiʿa, yāniʿa and nābiʿa rhyme.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ تَاجُ الْمُلُوكِ لِأَتْبَاعِهِ أَنْصِبُو الْحَبَائِلَ هُنَا وَأَوْسِعُوا دَائِرَةَ حَلْقَتِهَا وَيَكُونُ اجْتِمَاعُنَا عِنْدَ رَأْسِ الْحَلْقَةِ فِى الْمَكَانِ الْفُلَانِيِّ
sentences.tr: fa-qāla tāju al-mulūki li-atbāʿihi anṣibū al-ḥabāʾila hunā wa-awsiʿū dāʾirata ḥalqatihā wa-yakūnu ijtimāʿunā ʿinda raʾsi al-ḥalqati fī al-makāni al-fulāniyyi
sentences.l: And Tāj al-Mulūk said to his followers: Set-up the nets here, and widen the circle of their ring; and our gathering will be at the head of the ring, in the place such-and-such.
sentences.i: Tāj al-Mulūk said to his followers, “Set up the nets here and make their ring wide, and we will meet at the head of the ring, at such-and-such a place.”
sentences.n: anṣibū, “set up”, is read as form IV, as the text has it again in the next sentence (Classical uses form I, inṣibū); the print also drops the alif that normally follows the plural -ū. li-, “to”: qāla li-, “said to”. The hunt is a drive: nets are stretched in a great ring, the game is pressed inward, and the hunters meet where the ring closes. al-makān al-fulānī is the storyteller’s “such-and-such a place”.

sentences.t: فَامْتَثَلُوا أَمْرَهُ وَأَنْصَبُوا الْحَبَائِلَ وَأَوْسَعُوا دَائِرَةَ حَلْقَتِهَا فَاجْتَمَعَ فِيهَا شَيْءٌ كَثِيرٌ مِنْ أَصْنَافِ الْوُحُوشِ وَالْغِزْلَانِ إِلَى أَنْ ضَجَّتْ مِنْهُمُ الْوُحُوشُ وَتَنَافَرَتْ فِي وُجُوهِ الْخَيْلِ فَأَغْرَى عَلَيْهَا الْكِلَابَ وَالْفُهُودَ وَالصُّقُورَ ثُمَّ ضَرَبُوا الْوُحُوشَ بِالنُّشَّابِ فَأَصَابُوا مَقَاتِلَ الْوُحُوشِ وَمَا وَصَلُوا إِلَى آخِرِ الْحَلْقَةِ إِلَّا وَقَدْ أَخَذُوا مِنَ الْوُحُوشِ شَيْأً كَثِيرًا وَهَرَبَ الْبَاقِي
sentences.tr: fa-imtathalū amrahu wa-anṣabū al-ḥabāʾila wa-awsaʿū dāʾirata ḥalqatihā fa-ijtamaʿa fīhā shayʾun kathīrun min aṣnāfi al-wuḥūshi wa-al-ghizlāni ilā an ḍajjat minhumu al-wuḥūshu wa-tanāfarat fī wujūhi al-khayli fa-aghrā ʿalayhā al-kilāba wa-al-fuhūda wa-al-ṣuqūra thumma ḍarabū al-wuḥūsha bi-al-nushshābi fa-aṣābū maqātila al-wuḥūshi wa-mā waṣalū ilā ākhiri al-ḥalqati illā wa-qad akhadhū mina al-wuḥūshi shayʾan kathīran wa-haraba al-bāqī
sentences.l: And they complied-with his command, and set-up the nets and widened the circle of their ring; and there gathered in it a great deal of the kinds of the wild-beasts and the gazelles, until the wild-beasts cried-out from them and scattered in the faces of the horses; and he set on them the dogs and the cheetahs and the falcons; then they struck the wild-beasts with the arrows and hit the killing-places of the wild-beasts; and they did not reach the end of the ring except having taken of the wild-beasts a great deal; and the remainder fled.
sentences.i: They did as he commanded, set up the nets and spread the ring wide, and a great many beasts of every kind gathered inside it, gazelles among them, until the animals were crying out in terror of the hunters and bolting into the very faces of the horses. He loosed the hounds, the cheetahs and the falcons on them; then they shot the beasts with arrows and struck them in their vital parts, and by the time they reached the far end of the ring they had taken a great many. The rest escaped.
sentences.n: anṣabū, “they set up”, is form IV where Classical Arabic uses form I (naṣabū), a Middle Arabic touch. ḍajjat minhum, “cried out because of them”: min gives the cause. aghrā ʿalā, “set (hounds) on”. bi-, “with”: bi-al-nushshābi, “with arrows”. wa-mā waṣalū … illā wa-qad akhadhū, “they did not reach … except having already taken”, that is, by the time they reached. The print spells shayʾan as شيأ.

sentences.t: وَبَعْدَ ذَلِكَ نَزَلَ تَاجُ الْمُلُوكِ عَلَى الْمَاءِ وَأَحْضَرَ الصَّيْدَ وَقَسَّمَهُ وَأَفْرَدَ لِأَبِيهِ سُلَيْمَانَ شَاهْ خَاصَّ الْوُحُوشِ وَأَرْسَلَهُ إِلَيْهِ وَفَرَّقَ الْبَعْضَ عَلَى أَرْبَابِ دَوْلَتِهِ وَبَاتَ تِلْكَ اللَّيْلَةَ فِي ذَلِكَ الْمَكَانِ
sentences.tr: wa-baʿda dhālika nazala tāju al-mulūki ʿalā al-māʾi wa-aḥḍara al-ṣayda wa-qassamahu wa-afrada li-abīhi sulaymāna shāh khāṣṣa al-wuḥūshi wa-arsalahu ilayhi wa-farraqa al-baʿḍa ʿalā arbābi dawlatihi wa-bāta tilka al-laylata fī dhālika al-makāni
sentences.l: And after that Tāj al-Mulūk alighted by the water, and had the game brought and divided it, and set-apart for his father Sulaymān Shāh the choice of the wild-beasts and sent it to him, and distributed some among the lords of his state; and he passed-the-night that night in that place.
sentences.i: After that Tāj al-Mulūk made camp by the water, had the game brought in and divided it, setting aside the choicest beasts for his father, Sulaymān Shāh, and sending them to him, and sharing out some among the officers of his state; and he spent that night there.
sentences.n: The print again has شاة, a misprint for شاه, corrected here. nazala ʿalā al-māʾi, “alighted at the water”, camped beside it. li-, “for”: afrada li-abīhi, “set apart for his father”. khāṣṣ al-wuḥūsh, “the pick of the beasts”. arbāb dawlatihi, “the lords of his state”, are the officers of state.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا أَصْبَحَ الصَّبَاحُ أَقْبَلَتْ عَلَيْهِمْ قَافِلَةٌ كَبِيرَةٌ مُشْتَمِلَةٌ عَلَى عَبِيدٍ وَغِلْمَانٍ وَتُجَّارٍ فَنَزَلَتْ تِلْكَ الْقَافِلَةُ عَلَى الْمَاءِ وَالْخُضْرَةِ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā aṣbaḥa al-ṣabāḥu aqbalat ʿalayhim qāfilatun kabīratun mushtamilatun ʿalā ʿabīdin wa-ghilmānin wa-tujjārin fa-nazalat tilka al-qāfilatu ʿalā al-māʾi wa-al-khuḍrati
sentences.l: And when the morning came-to-be-morning, there came-upon them a caravan, great, comprising slaves and pages and merchants; and that caravan alighted by the water and the greenery.
sentences.i: In the morning a great caravan came upon them, made up of slaves, pages and merchants, and it halted by the water and the green.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا رَآهُمْ تَاجُ الْمُلُوكِ قَالَ لِبَعْضِ أَصْحَابِهِ أْتِنِي بِخَبَرِ هَؤُلَاءِ وَاسْأَلْهُمْ لِأَيِّ شَيْءٍ نَزَلُوا فِي هَذَا الْمَكَانِ فَلَمَّا تَوَجَّهَ إِلَيْهِمُ الرَّسُولُ قَالَ لَهُمْ أَخْبِرُونَا مَنْ أَنْتُمْ وَأَسْرِعُوا فِي رَدِّ الْجَوَابِ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā raʾāhum tāju al-mulūki qāla li-baʿḍi aṣḥābihi iʾtinī bi-khabari hāʾulāʾi wa-isʾalhum li-ayyi shayʾin nazalū fī hādhā al-makāni fa-lammā tawajjaha ilayhimu al-rasūlu qāla lahum akhbirūnā man antum wa-asriʿū fī raddi al-jawābi
sentences.l: And when Tāj al-Mulūk saw them, he said to one of his companions: Bring me (with) the news of these, and ask them for what thing they have alighted in this place. And when the messenger turned toward them, he said to them: Tell us who you are, and be-quick in the returning of the answer.
sentences.i: When Tāj al-Mulūk saw them, he said to one of his companions, “Bring me word of these people, and ask them why they have halted here.” When the messenger reached them he said, “Tell us who you are, and be quick with your answer.”
sentences.n: iʾtinī, “come to me”, is printed أتني, with the hamza on the alif; atā bi- is “bring”, the verb choosing the preposition, so iʾtinī bi-khabari is “bring me news of”. li-, “for”: li-ayyi shayʾin, “for what thing”, why.

sentences.t: فَقَالُوا لَهُ نَحْنُ تُجَّارٌ وَنَزَلْنَا هُنَا لِأَجْلِ الرَّاحَةِ لِأَنَّ الْمَنْزِلَ بَعِيدٌ عَلَيْنَا وَقَدْ نَزَلْنَا فِي هَذَا الْمَكَانِ لِأَنَّنَا مُطْمَئِنُّونَ بِالْمَلِكِ سُلَيْمَانَ شَاهْ وَوَلَدِهِ وَنَعْلَمُ أَنَّ كُلَّ مَنْ نَزَلَ عِنْدَهُ صَارَ فِي أَمَانٍ وَاطْمِئْنَانٍ وَمَعَنَا قُمَاشٌ نَفِيسٌ جِئْنَا بِهِ مِنْ أَجْلِ وَلَدِهِ تَاجِ الْمُلُوكِ
sentences.tr: fa-qālū lahu naḥnu tujjārun wa-nazalnā hunā li-ajli al-rāḥati li-anna al-manzila baʿīdun ʿalaynā wa-qad nazalnā fī hādhā al-makāni li-annanā muṭmaʾinnūna bi-al-maliki sulaymāna shāh wa-waladihi wa-naʿlamu anna kulla man nazala ʿindahu ṣāra fī amānin wa-iṭmiʾnānin wa-maʿanā qumāshun nafīsun jiʾnā bihi min ajli waladihi tāji al-mulūki
sentences.l: And they said to him: We are merchants, and we have alighted here for the sake of the rest, because the stopping-place is far for us; and we have alighted in this place because we are at-ease in the king Sulaymān Shāh and his son, and we know that everyone who alights near him comes-to-be in safety and security; and with us is cloth, precious, which we have come with for the sake of his son Tāj al-Mulūk.
sentences.i: They answered him, “We are merchants. We have halted here to rest, because the next stage is a long way off for us; and we chose this place because we trust in King Sulaymān Shāh and his son, and know that whoever halts in his land is safe and secure. We have precious fabrics with us, which we have brought for his son, Tāj al-Mulūk.”
sentences.n: li-ajli, li- “for” + ajl “sake”: “for the sake of”; li-anna, “because”. bi-, “in”: muṭmaʾinnūna bi-, “at ease in, trusting in”. jiʾnā bihi, jāʾa bi-, “come with”, that is, “we have brought it”. al-manzil is the next caravan stage. amān and iṭmiʾnān, “safety and security”, chime.

sentences.t: فَرَجَعَ الرَّسُولُ إِلَى ابْنِ الْمَلِكِ وَأَعْلَمَهُ بِحَقِيقَةِ الْحَالِ وَأَخْبَرَهُ بِمَا سَمِعَهُ مِنَ التُّجَّارِ فَقَالَ ابْنُ الْمَلِكِ إِذَا كَانَ مَعَهُمْ شَيْءٌ جَاؤُابِهِ مِنْ أَجْلِي فَمَا أَدْخُلُ الْمَدِينَةَ وَلَا أَرْحَلُ مِنْ هَذَا الْمَكَانِ حَتَّى أَسْتَعْرِضَهُ
sentences.tr: fa-rajaʿa al-rasūlu ilā ibni al-maliki wa-aʿlamahu bi-ḥaqīqati al-ḥāli wa-akhbarahu bi-mā samiʿahu mina al-tujjāri fa-qāla ibnu al-maliki idhā kāna maʿahum shayʾun jāʾū bihi min ajlī fa-mā adkhulu al-madīnata wa-lā arḥalu min hādhā al-makāni ḥattā astaʿriḍahu
sentences.l: And the messenger returned to the son of the king and informed him of the truth of the state, and told him of what he had heard from the merchants. And the son of the king said: If there is with them a thing they have come with for my sake, then I do not enter the city nor depart from this place until I have-it-displayed.
sentences.i: The messenger went back to the prince, told him how matters stood and repeated what he had heard from the merchants; and the prince said, “If they have something they have brought for me, I will not go back into the city or leave this place until I have had it laid out before me.”
sentences.n: The print has اى, a misprint for الى, “to”, corrected here. bi-, “of”: aʿlamahu bi- and akhbarahu bi-, “informed him of, told him of”. The print runs جاؤابه, “they brought it”, together. istaʿraḍa, “to have (goods) laid out for inspection”.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ رَكِبَ جَوَادَهُ وَسَارَ وَسَارَتْ مَمَالِيكُهُ خَلْفَهُ إِلَى أَنْ أَشْرَفَ عَلَى الْقَافِلَةِ فَقَامَ لَهُ التُّجَّارُ وَدَعَوْالَهُ بِالنَّصْرِ وَالْإِقْبَالِ وَدَوَامِ الْعِزِّ وَالْإِفْضَالِ وَقَدْ ضُرِبَتْ لَهُ خَيْمَةٌ مِنَ الْأَطْلَسِ الْأَحْمَرِ مُزَرْكَشَةٌ بِالدُّرِّ وَالْجَوْهَرِ وَفَرَشُوا لَهُ مَقْعَدًا سُلْطَانِيًّا فَوْقَ بِسَاطٍ مِنَ الْحَرِيرِ وَصَدْرُهُ مُزَرْكَشٌ بِالزُّمُرُّدِ
sentences.tr: thumma rakiba jawādahu wa-sāra wa-sārat mamālīkuhu khalfahu ilā an ashrafa ʿalā al-qāfilati fa-qāma lahu al-tujjāru wa-daʿaw lahu bi-al-naṣri wa-al-iqbāli wa-dawāmi al-ʿizzi wa-al-ifḍāli wa-qad ḍuribat lahu khaymatun mina al-aṭlasi al-aḥmari muzarkashatun bi-al-durri wa-al-jawhari wa-farashū lahu maqʿadan sulṭāniyyan fawqa bisāṭin mina al-ḥarīri wa-ṣadruhu muzarkashun bi-al-zumurrudi
sentences.l: Then he mounted his steed and journeyed, and his mamlūks journeyed behind him, until he looked-down upon the caravan; and the merchants rose for him and prayed for him for the victory and the good-fortune and the lasting of the might and the bounty. And there had been pitched for him a tent of the satin, the red, embroidered with the pearls and the jewels; and they spread for him a seat, sultanly, upon a carpet of the silk, and its upper-end embroidered with the emerald.
sentences.i: Then he mounted his horse and rode off, his mamlūks riding behind him, until he came in sight of the caravan. The merchants rose to greet him and called down blessings on him: victory and good fortune, lasting glory and bounty. A tent of red satin worked with pearls and jewels had been pitched for him, and they set out a seat fit for a sultan on a silk carpet whose head was embroidered with emeralds.
sentences.n: daʿā lahu bi-, “pray for him for (a thing)”: bi- names what is asked for; the print runs ودعواله, “and they prayed for him”, together. iqbāl and ifḍāl rhyme. muzarkash, “embroidered, worked with gold thread”. The ṣadr, “chest”, of a carpet or a room is its upper end, the place of honour.

sentences.t: فَجَلَسَ تَاجُ الْمُلُوكِ وَوَقَفَتِ الْمَمَالِيكُ فِي خِدْمَتِهِ وَأَرْسَلَ إِلَى التُّجَّارِ وَأَمَرَهُمْ أَنْ يُحْضِرُوا بِجَمِيعِ مَا مَعَهُمْ فَأَقْبَلَتْ عَلَيْهِ التُّجَّارُ بِبَضَائِعِهِمْ فَاسْتَعْرَضَ جَمِيعَ بِضَاعَتِهِمْ وَأَخَذَ مِنْهَا مَا يَصْلُحُ لَهُ وَوَفَّى لَهُمْ بِالثَّمَنِ
sentences.tr: fa-jalasa tāju al-mulūki wa-waqafati al-mamālīku fī khidmatihi wa-arsala ilā al-tujjāri wa-amarahum an yuḥḍirū bi-jamīʿi mā maʿahum fa-aqbalat ʿalayhi al-tujjāru bi-baḍāʾiʿihim fa-istaʿraḍa jamīʿa biḍāʿatihim wa-akhadha minhā mā yaṣluḥu lahu wa-waffā lahum bi-al-thamani
sentences.l: And Tāj al-Mulūk sat, and the mamlūks stood in his service; and he sent to the merchants and commanded them that they bring (with) all that was with them; and the merchants came-forward to him with their wares, and he had-displayed all their merchandise, and took of it what was fitting for him, and paid them in-full the price.
sentences.i: Tāj al-Mulūk took his seat, his mamlūks standing in attendance, and sent to the merchants, ordering them to bring everything they had. The merchants came before him with their wares; he looked over all their goods, took what suited him, and paid them the price in full.
sentences.n: The print has اى again, a misprint for الى, corrected here. aḥḍara bi-, “bring”, takes a bi- here as jāʾa bi- does, where Classical aḥḍara needs none. bi-, “with”: bi-baḍāʾiʿihim, “with their wares”; waffā lahum bi-al-thamani, “paid them the price in full”. al-tujjār, a broken plural, takes a feminine verb, aqbalat.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ رَكِبَ وَأَرَادَأَنْ يَسِيرَ فَلَاحَتْ مِنْهُ الْتِفَاتَةٌ إِلَى الْقَافِلَةِ فَرَأَي شَابًّا جَمِيلَ الشَّبَابِ نَظِيفَ الثِّيَابِ ظَرِيفَ الْمَعَانِي بِجَبِينٍ أَزْهَرَ وَوَجْهٍ أَقْمَرَ إِلَّا أَنَّ ذَلِكَ الشَّابَّ قَدْ تَغَيَّرَتْ مَحَاسِنُهُ وَعَلَاهُ الِاصْفِرَارُ مِنْ فُرْقَةِ الْأَحْبَابِ
sentences.tr: thumma rakiba wa-arāda an yasīra fa-lāḥat minhu iltifātatun ilā al-qāfilati fa-raʾā shābban jamīla al-shabābi naẓīfa al-thiyābi ẓarīfa al-maʿānī bi-jabīnin azhara wa-wajhin aqmara illā anna dhālika al-shābba qad taghayyarat maḥāsinuhu wa-ʿalāhu al-iṣfirāru min furqati al-aḥbābi
sentences.l: Then he mounted and wanted to go; and there appeared from him a turning-glance toward the caravan, and he saw a youth, beautiful of youth, clean of clothes, elegant of qualities, with a brow radiant and a face moon-bright; except that that youth — his beauties had changed, and the yellowness had come-over him from the parting of the loved-ones.
sentences.i: Then he mounted and was about to ride off when he happened to glance back at the caravan, and saw a young man in the full beauty of youth, neatly dressed and graceful in manner, with a radiant brow and a face like the moon; but that young man’s good looks had faded, and the pallor of parting from those he loved had come over him.
sentences.n: lāḥat minhu iltifātatun, “a glance came from him”: he happened to look round. The print spells raʾā with a final yāʾ (فرأي), and runs وارادان, “and wanted to”, together. bi-, “with”: bi-jabīnin azhara, “with a radiant brow”. Rhymed prose: al-shabāb, al-thiyāb … al-aḥbāb; azhar and aqmar.

sentences.t: وَأَدْرَكَ شَهْرَ زَادَ الصَّبَاحُ فَسَكَتَتْ عَنِ الْكَلَامِ الْمُبَاحِ
sentences.tr: wa-adraka shahrazāda al-ṣabāḥu fa-sakatat ʿani al-kalāmi al-mubāḥi
sentences.l: And the morning overtook Shahrazād, and she fell silent from the permitted speech.
sentences.i: Morning overtook Shahrazād, and she fell silent, leaving the permitted speech.
sentences.n: The print sets the name as two words here, شهر زاد.
